Core Thesis

On November 1st, a Learjet 60 carrying nine people crashed in Florida after experiencing severe weather and technical difficulties at 35,000 feet, with the NTSB classifying it as a Loss of Control in Flight (LOCI) incident involving icing, turbulence, and potential speed-related aerodynamic issues.

Key Points

  • The aircraft descended from 35,250 feet to 8,750 feet in just over one minute (approximately 20,000 feet per minute), with the crew reporting an overspeed condition before impact; all nine occupants were killed, but no ground casualties occurred.
  • At high altitudes, the Learjet 60's safe speed window narrows significantly due to thin air density—the aircraft must fly between stall speed (too slow) and Mach 0.81 (approximately 880 km/h), leaving minimal margin for error when wind shear or turbulence is present.
  • The NTSB is investigating multiple contributing factors including severe weather (icing and moderate turbulence), potential structural failure, and aerodynamic phenomena such as "shock stall" (MachTac), where shock waves form on the wing and degrade control surface effectiveness.
  • Florida thunderstorms can exceed 40,000 feet in altitude and present extreme vertical wind shear, which may have destabilized the aircraft and pushed it outside its safe flight envelope during the attempted altitude climb.

    • Takeaways

  • Understanding that aircraft accidents rarely result from a single cause—instead, they involve a cascade of factors (weather, aircraft design limits, crew response) that combine to exceed safety margins.
  • The concept of "coffin corner" (where minimum and maximum speed limits converge at extreme altitudes) illustrates why high-altitude flight in adverse weather presents unique hazards that ground-based observers may not fully appreciate.
  • The ongoing NTSB investigation will examine maintenance records and flight data to determine whether structural failure, pilot error, or aerodynamic stall played the primary role—findings that may inform future aviation safety protocols.

Many people unconsciously adopt dysfunctional parenting styles toward their inner child—dismissive, comparative, guilt-tripping, inconsistent, codependent, or martyr-like—which sabotages their goals, keeps them in survival responses, and prevents authentic self-expression and growth.

Key Points

  • **Dismissive/neglectful parenting**: Invalidating the inner child's hopes and dreams by labeling them as stupid, unrealistic, or reckless, leading to shame-based avoidance of feelings and eventual self-sabotage.
  • **Comparison and guilt-tripping patterns**: Using comparisons to others or guilt manipulation to convince the inner child it's behind, unsafe, and selfish for wanting more—creating learned helplessness over time.
  • **Inconsistent and codependent dynamics**: Showing up sporadically for yourself while simultaneously shrinking your identity and boundaries to avoid upsetting others, resulting in constant self-sacrifice and loss of authenticity.
  • **Survival mode consequences**: These parenting patterns keep adults locked in fight, flight, freeze, or fawn nervous system responses, manifesting as overspending, binge eating, excessive scrolling, and other self-soothing avoidance behaviors.
  • **Martyr identity**: Tying self-worth to suffering and pain as "proof" of deservingness, which blocks the inner child from attempting growth or expansion.

    • Takeaways

  • Identify which parenting style(s) you use with your inner child and notice how they show up in daily self-sabotage behaviors and relationship patterns.
  • Begin a daily nervous system regulation practice (grounding, breathwork, somatic work) to step out of constant survival responses and create safety for inner child reparenting.
